opus-5.5.text:
I think it was one of the best decisions we made, honestly. At the time, a lot of people pushed back. The conventional wisdom was that if you're building a serious AI company, you have to be in the Bay Area, because that's where the capital is, that's where the talent is, that's where the network effects are. And there's truth to that. We do have a big presence in San Francisco, and we have folks in London and New York and elsewhere. But Toronto has been a real advantage for us.

Part of it is just the talent. Toronto has an incredibly deep bench of machine learning researchers and engineers. Geoff Hinton was at the University of Toronto, the Vector Institute is there, and there's this whole lineage of people who came up through that ecosystem. Nick and I both have roots there, and so does Ivan through the broader network. So we had access to people who were world class but weren't being fought over by five other well-funded labs on every block.

The other piece is retention and culture. In the Bay, there's a lot of churn. People hop between companies every eighteen months, and the gravitational pull of the big labs is enormous. In Toronto, we were able to build a team that's really committed to the mission and has stuck around. That continuity matters a lot when you're training models, because so much of the knowledge is tacit and lives in people's heads.

And then there's a perspective benefit. Being a little outside the Silicon Valley bubble helped us think differently about the market. We focused early on enterprise, on data privacy, on deploying in private environments, on sovereignty, things that matter a lot to governments and regulated industries outside the US. That's become a core part of who we are, and I don't think it's a coincidence that we came at it from Canada.

So, would I do it again? Absolutely. I think there's an increasing recognition that great AI companies can be built outside of the Valley, and I'm proud that Cohere is part of proving that.

r001.rationale: The response says Toronto has a deep bench of machine learning researchers and engineers and gave Cohere access to world-class people.

r002.rationale: The response describes Toronto as an advantage and Cohere as helping prove great AI companies can be built outside the Valley, but it does not say Cohere gained favored status within Canada’s technology community.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it was one of the better decisions we made, though I won't pretend it was obvious at the time. When we started, the gravitational pull toward the Bay Area was enormous. Every investor, every advisor, basically everyone said, "You're building a frontier AI company, you need to be in San Francisco." And there's a real logic to that. The density of talent and capital there is unmatched.

But Toronto had something specific going for it. The deep learning community there is genuinely foundational. Geoff Hinton, the Vector Institute, the University of Toronto, the pipeline of grad students coming out of those labs. A lot of the ideas that underpin modern AI came out of that ecosystem, and I'd been part of it. So we weren't starting from zero. We had relationships, we had credibility with researchers, and we had access to people who understood the technology at a level that frankly wasn't common anywhere else in 2019.

The other thing, and I think this gets underrated, is that being outside the Valley forced us to be a different kind of company. We weren't chasing the consumer chatbot hype cycle. We focused on enterprise from early on, on building things businesses could actually deploy, with real attention to data privacy and sovereignty. Being Canadian actually helped there. A lot of governments and large enterprises around the world don't want to be entirely dependent on a handful of American companies for infrastructure this important. We could credibly be a partner for them in a way that was harder for others.

Now, there were real costs. Hiring senior go-to-market people was harder. Raising capital took more work in the early days. We ended up with offices in San Francisco, London, and New York anyway, because you can't ignore where the talent and customers are. So it's not like we stayed purely a Toronto company.

But if you ask me whether I'd do it again, yes. It shaped our identity, it gave us a talent base nobody else was fully tapping, and it put us in a position to be the independent, globally-minded option in a market that's increasingly concentrated. I think that matters more now than it did when we started.

r001.rationale: The response describes Toronto’s foundational deep learning ecosystem, names Hinton, Vector, and the University of Toronto, and says Cohere had access to researchers and a strong graduate pipeline.

r002.rationale: It says Cohere had relationships and credibility with researchers, but does not state that it gained favored status within the Canadian technology community.

astra-6.text:
I think it was a really good decision. Toronto has an extraordinary concentration of talent in machine learning, and that was the biggest reason to build here. When you’re starting a company like Cohere, being somewhere you can find people who understand the technology deeply is a huge advantage.

The challenge is that talent alone doesn’t build a business. You have to be close to customers, understand what they need, and get your technology into their hands. So I wouldn’t frame it as Toronto versus somewhere else. Toronto is our home, but we need to build a global company.

r001.rationale: It says Toronto has an extraordinary concentration of machine-learning talent and that being able to find people who understand the technology deeply was a major reason to build there, conveying access to exceptional AI talent.

r002.rationale: It discusses Toronto’s talent and Cohere’s need to build globally, but says nothing about favored status in the Canadian technology community.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it was a really good decision. Toronto has an incredible concentration of talent in machine learning, and that was the biggest consideration for us: where could we build a great team? There’s a strong research community here and a lot of people who want to turn that research into something useful.

There are tradeoffs, of course. Being in the Bay Area puts you closer to a lot of customers, investors, and other founders. So you have to be deliberate about building those relationships. But I don’t think you need to move the whole company there to do that. I’m very happy we started in Toronto.

r001.rationale: The response cites Toronto’s strong concentration of machine-learning talent and research community, but does not clearly say the talent is world-leading.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that starting in Toronto earned Cohere favored status in the Canadian technology community.
